The series above converges for any complex number a with $|a| < 1$ (see Exercise 3 of Chapter 12). The broader generalization, for any integer k $\geq 1$ , is

$$
\frac {1}{k !} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} (n + k) (n + k - 1) \dots (n + 1) a ^ {n} = \frac {1}{(1 - a) ^ {k + 1}},
$$

(13.12)

for any complex number a with $|a| < 1$.

Consider then a Z transform $\hat{X}$ that has a pole at p of multiplicity m and no zeros. Since the pole p cannot belong to RoC, the RoC is either

$$
\{z \in \mathbb {C} \mid | z | > | p | \} \text {o r} \{z \in \mathbb {C} \mid | z | < | p | \}.
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

In the first case we expand $\hat{X}$ in a series involving only the terms $z^{-n}, n\geq 0,$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {X} (z) = \frac {1}{(z - p) ^ {m}} \\ = \frac {z ^ {- m}}{(1 - p z ^ {- 1}) ^ {m}} \\ = z ^ {- m} \frac {1}{(m - 1) !} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} (m + n - 1) \dots (n + 1) \left(p z ^ {- 1}\right) ^ {n}, \text {u s i n g} (1 3. 1 2) \\ = \frac {1}{(m - 1) !} \sum_ {k = m} ^ {\infty} (k - 1) \dots (k - m + 1) p ^ {k - m} z ^ {- k}, \text {d e f i n i n g} k = n + m \\ \end{array}
$$

and the series converges for any z with $|z|>|p|$. We can match the coefficients of the powers of z in the Z transform definition,

$$
\hat {X} (z) = \sum_ {k = - \infty} ^ {\infty} x (k) z ^ {- k},
$$

from which we can recognize that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall k \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad x (k) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & k < m \\ \frac {1}{(m - 1) !} (k - 1) \dots (k - m + 1) p ^ {k - m}, & k \geq m \end{array} \right. \\ = \frac {1}{(m - 1) !} (k - 1) \dots (k - m + 1) p ^ {k - m} u (k - m). \\ \end{array}
$$

(13.13)

(13.13)

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {X} (z) = \frac {1}{(z - p) ^ {m}} \\ = \frac {1}{(- p) ^ {m}} \frac {1}{(1 - p ^ {- 1} z) ^ {m}} \\ = \frac {1}{(- p) ^ {m}} \frac {1}{(m - 1) !} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} (m + n - 1) \dots (n + 1) \left(p ^ {- 1} z\right) ^ {n}, \text {u s i n g} (1 3. 1 2) \\ = \frac {(- 1) ^ {m}}{(m - 1) !} \sum_ {k = - \infty} ^ {0} (m - k - 1) \dots (1 - k) p ^ {k - m} z ^ {- k}, \text {d e f i n i n g} k = - n, \\ \end{array}

and the series converges for any z with $|z| < |p|$. Again, we match powers of z in the Z transform definition to get

$$

(13.14)

with $RoC = \{z\in \mathbb{C} \mid |z| > 2\}$ . Then, by (13.13), $\hat{X}$ is the Z transform of the signal

\forall k \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad x (k) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & k < 2 \\ (k - 1) 2 ^ {k - 2}, & k \geq 2 \end{array} \right..

Suppose

\hat {Y} (z) = \frac {1}{(z - 2) ^ {2}}

with $RoC = \{z\in \mathbb{C} \mid |z| < 2\}$ . Then, by (13.14), $\hat{Y}$ is the Z transform of the signal

$$

Since the unit circle $\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid|z|=1\} \subset RoC$ , the DTFT of y is defined and given by

\forall \omega \in \mathbb {R}, \quad Y (\omega) = \hat {Y} \left(e ^ {i \omega}\right) = \frac {1}{\left(e ^ {i \omega} - 2\right) ^ {2}}.

Now that we know how to inverse transform all the terms of the partial fraction expansion, we can generalize the method used in example 13.15 to calculate the inverse Z transform

of any $\hat{X}$ of the form

where $\hat{W}$ is strictly proper.

$$
\forall n, \quad x (n) = c _ {m + l - N} \delta (n + m + l - N) + \dots + c _ {0} \delta (n) + w (n).

Working now with $\hat{Y}$ , step 1 yields

\forall n, \quad w (n) = - 5 (n - 1) (- 2) ^ {n - 2} u (n - 2) + 9 (- 2) ^ {n - 1} u (n - 1),

## 13.5.2 Inverse Laplace transform

The procedure to calculate the inverse Laplace transform is virtually identical. Suppose the Laplace transform $\hat{X}$ is a rational polynomial

$$
\hat {X} (s) = \frac {a _ {M} s ^ {M} + \cdots + a _ {0}}{s ^ {N} + b _ {N - 1} s ^ {N - 1} + \cdots + b _ {0}}.
$$

We follow Steps 1 and 2 above. We divide through in case $M\geq N$ to obtain

$$
\hat {X} (s) = c _ {M - N} s ^ {M - N} + \dots + c _ {0} + \hat {W} (s),
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
\hat {X} (s) = c _ {M - N} s ^ {M - N} + \dots + c _ {0} + \hat {W} (s),
$$

where $\hat{W}$ is strictly proper. We carry out the partial fraction expansion of $\hat{W}.$ Knowing $RoC(x)$ , we can again infer the region of convergence of each term. We then obtain the inverse Laplace transform term by term using table 13.3,

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad x (t) = c _ {m - n} \delta^ {(M - N)} (t) + \dots + c _ {0} \delta (t) + w (t).
$$

Here w is the inverse Laplace transform of $\hat{W}$ , $\delta$ is the Dirac delta function, and $\delta^{(i)}$ is the ith derivative of the Dirac delta function. $^{1}$

$^{1}$ The derivative of $\delta$ is a function only in a formal sense, and we obtain its Laplace transform using the differentiation property in table 13.4.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {X} (s) = \frac {s ^ {3} + s ^ {2} + s + 1}{s (s + 2) ^ {2}} \\ = 1 + \frac {- 3 s ^ {2} - 3 s + 1}{s (s + 2) ^ {2}} \\ = 1 + \frac {1 / 4}{s} + \frac {- 1 3 / 4}{s + 2} + \frac {5 / 2}{(s + 2) ^ {2}}. \\ \end{array}

We now use table 13.3 to obtain the inverse Laplace transform of each term. In case (1), the continuous-time signal is the anti-causal signal

$$
\forall t, \quad x (t) = \delta (t) - \frac {1}{4} u (- t) + \frac {1 3}{4} e ^ {- 2 t} u (- t) - \frac {5}{2} t e ^ {- 2 t} u (- t).

In case (2), it is the two-sided signal,

\forall t, \quad x (t) = \delta (t) - \frac {1}{4} u (- t) - \frac {1 3}{4} e ^ {- 2 t} u (t) + \frac {5}{2} t e ^ {- 2 t} u (t).

In case (3), it is the causal signal,

\forall t, \quad x (t) = \delta (t) + \frac {1}{4} u (t) - \frac {1 3}{4} e ^ {- 2 t} u (t) + \frac {5}{2} t e ^ {- 2 t} u (t).

## 13.6 Steady state response

Although it has been a fair amount of work, being able to compute an inverse transform for an arbitrary rational polynomial proves useful. Our first use will be to study the stead state response of a causal and stable LTI system that has a sinusoidal input that starts at time zero.

If the input to an LTI system is a complex exponential,

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad x (t) = e ^ {i \omega t},
$$

then the output y is an exponential of the same frequency but with amplitude and phase given by $H(\omega),$

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad y (t) = H (\omega) e ^ {i \omega t},
$$

where H is the frequency response. However, this result requires the exponential input to start at $t=-\infty$ . In practice, of course, an input may start at some finite time, say at $t=0$ but this result does not describe the output if the input is

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad x (t) = e ^ {i \omega t} u (t).
$$

(13.17)

We will see that if the system is stable and causal, $^{2}$ then the output y decomposes into two parts, a transient output and a steady state output,

$$
y = y _ {t r} + y _ {s s},
$$

where the transient becomes vanishingly small for large t. That is,

$$
\lim _ {t \rightarrow \infty} y _ {t r} (t) = 0.
$$

Moreover, the steady state signal is the exponential,

$$
\forall t, \quad y _ {s s} (t) = H (\omega) e ^ {i \omega t} u (t).
$$

(13.18)

Thus for stable systems, we can use the frequency response to describe the eventual output to sinusoidal signals that start at some finite time.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
(13.18)

Thus for stable systems, we can use the frequency response to describe the eventual output to sinusoidal signals that start at some finite time.

For the special case $\omega=0$ , the input (13.17) is the unit step, $x=u$ , and $y_{ss}=H(0)u$ . So for stable systems, the steady state response to a unit step input is a step of size $H(0)$ .

$^{2}$ This result can be generalized to non-causal systems, but causal systems will be sufficient for our purposes.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
($H(0)$ is called the dc gain.） This case is important in the design of feedback control, considered in the next chapter.

Let h be the impulse response and $\hat{H}$ be the Laplace transform of a stable and causal LTI system. We assume for simplicity that $\hat{H}$ is a strictly proper rational polynomial all of whose poles have multiplicity one,

$$
\hat {H} (s) = \frac {A (s)}{\left(s - p _ {1}\right) \cdots \left(s - p _ {N}\right)}.
$$

Because the system is causal, RoC(h) has the form

$$
R o C (h) = \{s \mid R e \{s \} > q \},
$$

where q is the largest real part of any pole. Since the system is stable, q<0, so that the region of convergence includes the imaginary axis.

From table 13.3 the Laplace transform $\hat{X}$ of the signal (13.17) is

$$
\hat {X} (s) = \frac {1}{s - i \omega},
$$

The Laplace transform of the output $y=h * x$ is

$$
\hat {Y} = \hat {H} \hat {X},
$$

with

$$
R o C (y) \supset R o C (h) \cap R o C (x) = \{s \in \mathbb {C} \mid R e \{s \} > 0 \}.
$$

The partial fraction expansion of $\hat{Y}$ is

$$
\hat {Y} (s) = \hat {H} (s) \hat {X} (s) = \frac {A (s)}{\left(s - p _ {1}\right) \cdots \left(s - p _ {N}\right)} \cdot \frac {1}{s - i \omega}
$$

(13.19)

$$
= \frac {R _ {1}}{s - p _ {1}} + \dots + \frac {R _ {N}}{s - p _ {N}} + \frac {R _ {\omega}}{s - i \omega}.
$$

(13.20)
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
= \frac {R _ {1}}{s - p _ {1}} + \dots + \frac {R _ {N}}{s - p _ {N}} + \frac {R _ {\omega}}{s - i \omega}.
$$

(13.20)

Because everything is causal, each term must be causal, so from table 13.3 we obtain

$$
\forall t, \quad y (t) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {N} R _ {k} e ^ {p _ {k} t} u (t) + R _ {\omega} e ^ {i \omega t} u (t).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
We decompose $y=y_{tr}+y_{ss}$ , with

$$
\forall t, \quad y _ {t r} (t) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {N} R _ {k} e ^ {p _ {k} t} u (t),
$$

$$
\forall t, \quad y _ {s s} (t) = R _ {\omega} e ^ {i \omega t} u (t).
$$

Since $Re\{p_{k}\} < 0$ for $k = 1,\dots,N,$

$$
\lim _ {t \rightarrow \infty} y _ {t r} (t) = 0.
$$

Thus, the steady-state response $y_{ss}$ is eventually all that is left.

Finally, the residue $R_{\omega}$ is obtained by multiplying both sides of (13.19) by $s-i\omega$ and evaluating at $s=i\omega$ to get $R_{\omega}=\hat{H}(i\omega)=H(\omega)$ , so that

$$
\forall t, \quad y _ {s s} (t) = H (\omega) e ^ {i \omega t} u (t).
$$

This analysis reveals several interesting features of the total response y. First, from (13.20) we see the poles $p_{1},\dots,p_{N}$ of the transfer function contribute to the transient response $y_{tr}$ , and the pole of the input $\hat{X}$ at i $\omega$ contributes to the steady state response. Second we can determine how quickly the transient response dies down. The transient response is

$$
\forall t, \quad y _ {t r} (t) = R _ {1} e ^ {p _ {1} t} u (t) + \dots + R _ {N} e ^ {p _ {N} t} u (t).
$$

The magnitude of the terms is

$$
\left| R _ {1} \right| e ^ {R e \left\{p _ {1} \right\} t}, \dots , \left| R _ {N} \right| e ^ {R e \left\{p _ {N} \right\} t}.
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Each term decreases exponentially with $t$ , since the real parts of the poles are negative. The slowest decrease is due to the pole with the least negative part. Thus the pole of the stable, causal transfer function with the least negative part determines how fast the transient response goes to zero. Indeed for large $t$ , we can approximate the response $y$ as

$$
y (t) \approx R _ {i} e ^ {p _ {i} t} + H (\omega) e ^ {i \omega t},
$$

where $p_{i}$ is the pole with the largest (least negative) real part.

There is a similar result for discrete-time systems, and it is obtained in the same way. Suppose an exponential input

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad x (n) = e ^ {i \omega n} u (n),
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
is applied to a stable and causal system with impulse response h, transfer function $\hat{H}$ , and frequency response H. Then the output y=h $* x$ can again be decomposed as

$$
\forall n, \quad y (n) = y _ {t r} (n) + y _ {s s} (n),
$$

where the transient $y_{tr}(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ , and the steady state response is

$$
\forall n, \quad y _ {s s} (n) = \hat {H} \left(e ^ {i \omega}\right) e ^ {i \omega n} u (n) = H (\omega) e ^ {i \omega n} u (n).
$$

For large n, the transient response decays exponentially as $p_{i}^{n}$ , i.e.

$$
y (n) \approx R _ {i} p _ {i} ^ {n} + y _ {s s} (n),
$$

where $p_{i}$ is the pole with the largest magnitude (which must be less than one, since the system is stable).

## 13.7 Linear difference and differential equations

Many natural and man-made systems can be modeled as linear differential equations or difference equations. We have seen that when such systems are initially at rest, they are LTI systems. Hence, we can use their transfer functions (which are Z transforms or Laplace transforms) to analyze the response of these systems to external inputs.

However, physical systems are often not initially at rest. Dealing with non-zero initial conditions introduces some complexity in the analysis. Mathematicians call such systems with non-zero initial conditions initial value problems. We can adapt our methods to deal with initial conditions. The rest of this chapter is devoted to these methods.

Example 13.19: In example 13.8 we considered the LTI system described by the difference equation

$$
y (n) - 0. 9 y (n - 1) = x (n).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Example 13.19: In example 13.8 we considered the LTI system described by the difference equation

$$
y (n) - 0. 9 y (n - 1) = x (n).
$$

The transfer function of this system is $\hat{H} (z)=z /(z-0.9).$ If the system is initially at rest, we can calculate its response y from its Z transform $\hat{Y}=\hat{H}\hat{X}.$ For instance, if the input is the unit step, $\hat{X} (z)=z /(z-1),$

$$
\hat {Y} (z) = \frac {z ^ {2}}{(z - 0 . 9) (z - 1)} = \frac {- 9 z}{z - 0 . 9} + \frac {1 0 z}{z - 1},
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
and so $y ( n )=-9(0. 9)^{n}+1 0, n \geq 0.$

We cannot use the transfer function, however, to determine the response if the initial condition at time n=0 is y(-1) = $\bar{y} (-1)$ , and the input is x(n)=0, n $\geq 0$ . The response to this initial condition is

$$
y (n) = \bar {y} (- 1) (0. 9) ^ {n + 1}, n \geq - 1.
$$

We can check that this expression is correct by verifying that it satisfies both the initial condition and the difference equation.

If the initial condition is $y(-1)=\bar{y}(-1)$ and the input is a unit step, the response turns out to be the sum of the response due to the input (with zero initial condition) and the response due to the initial condition (with zero input),

$$
y (n) = \left[ - 9 (0. 9) ^ {n} + 1 0 \right] + \left[ \bar {y} (- 1) (0. 9) ^ {n + 1} \right], n \geq 0.
$$

For small values of n the response depends heavily on the initial condition, especially if $\overline{{y}} ( 0 )$ is large. Because this system is stable, the effect of the initial condition becomes vanishingly small for large n.

## An LTI difference equation has the form

$$
y (n) + a _ {1} y (n - 1) + \dots + a _ {m} y (n - m) = b _ {0} x (n) + \dots + b _ {k} x (n - k), n \geq 0.
$$

(13.21)

We interpret this equation as describing a causal discrete-time LTI system in which $x(n)$ is the input and $y(n)$ is the output at time n. The $a_{i}$ and $b_{j}$ are constant coefficients that specify the system.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
(13.21)

We interpret this equation as describing a causal discrete-time LTI system in which $x(n)$ is the input and $y(n)$ is the output at time n. The $a_{i}$ and $b_{j}$ are constant coefficients that specify the system.

We have used difference equations before. In section 8.2.1 we used this form and the discrete time Fourier transform to find the frequency response of this system. In section 9.5 we showed how to realize such systems as IIR filters. In example 13.19 we used the transfer function to find the response. But in all these cases, we had to assume that the system was initially at rest. We now develop a method to find the response for arbitrary initial conditions.

We assume the input signal x starts at some finite time, which we take to be zero, $x ( n )= 0,n<0.$ We wish to calculate $y ( n ),n\geq0.$ From (13.21) we can see that we need to be given m initial conditions,

$$
y (- 1) = \bar {y} (- 1), \dots , y (- m) = \bar {y} (- m).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Given the input signal and these initial conditions, there is a straightforward procedure to calculate the output response y(n), n $\geq0$ : Rewrite (13.21) as

$$
y (n) = - a _ {1} y (n - 1) - \dots - a _ {m} y (n - m) + b _ {0} x (n) + \dots + b _ {k} x (n - k),
$$

(13.22)

and recursively use (13.22) to obtain $y(0),y(1),y(2),\dots$ For n=0, (13.22) yields

$$
\begin{array}{l} y (0) = - a _ {1} y (- 1) - \dots - a _ {m} y (- m) + b _ {0} x (0) + \dots + b _ {k} x (- k) \\ = - a _ {1} \bar {y} (- 1) - \dots - a _ {m} \bar {y} (- m) + b _ {0} x (0). \\ \end{array}
$$

All the terms on the right are known from the initial conditions and the input $x(0)$ , so we can calculate $y ( 0 )$ . Next, taking n=1 in (13.22),

$$
y (1) = - a _ {1} y (0) + \dots + a _ {m} y (1 - m) + b _ {0} x (1) + \dots + b _ {k} x (1 - k).
$$

All the terms on the right are known either from the given data or from precalculated values— $y ( 0 )$ in this case. Proceeding in this way we can calculate the remaining values of the output sequence $y ( 2 ) , y ( 3 ) , \cdots$ , one at a time.

We now use the Z transform to calculate the entire output sequence. Multiplying both sides of (13.21) by $u(n)$ , the unit step, gives us a relation that holds among signals whose domain is $\mathbb{Z}$ :
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
We now use the Z transform to calculate the entire output sequence. Multiplying both sides of (13.21) by $u(n)$ , the unit step, gives us a relation that holds among signals whose domain is $\mathbb{Z}$ :

$$
\begin{array}{l} y (n) u (n) + a _ {1} y (n - 1) u (n) + \dots + a _ {m} y (n - m) u (n) \\ = b _ {0} x (n) u (n) + \dots + b _ {k} x (n - k) u (n), n \in \mathbb {Z}. \\ \end{array}
$$

We can now take the Z transforms of both sides. We multiply both sides by $z^{-n}$ and sum,

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n) z ^ {- n} + a _ {1} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n - 1) z ^ {- n} + \dots + a _ {m} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n - m) z ^ {- n} \\ = b _ {0} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n) z ^ {- n} + \dots + b _ {k} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n - k) z ^ {- n}. \\ \end{array}
$$

(13.23)

Define

$$
\hat {X} (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n) z ^ {- n}, \quad \hat {Y} (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n) z ^ {- n}.
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Each sum in (13.23) can be expressed in terms of $\hat{Y}$ or $\hat{X}.$ In evaluating the Z transforms of the signals $y(n-1)u(n),y(n-2)u(n),\cdots$ we need to include the initial conditions:

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n - 1) z ^ {- n} = \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {0} + z ^ {- 1} \sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} y (n - 1) z ^ {- (n - 1)} = \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {0} + z ^ {- 1} \hat {Y} (z),
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n - 2) z ^ {- n} = \bar {y} (- 2) z ^ {0} + \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- 1} + z ^ {- 2} \sum_ {n = 2} ^ {\infty} y (n - 2) z ^ {- (n - 2)} \\ = \bar {y} (- 2) z ^ {0} + \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- 1} + z ^ {- 2} \hat {Y} (z), \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n - m) z ^ {- n} = \bar {y} (- m) z ^ {0} + \dots + \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- (m - 1)} + z ^ {- m} \sum_ {n = m} ^ {\infty} y (n - m) z ^ {- (n - m)} \\ = \bar {y} (- m) z ^ {0} + \dots + \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- (m - 1)} + z ^ {- m} \hat {Y} (z). \\ \end{array}
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Because $x(n)=0,n<0$ , by assumption, the sums on the right in (13.23) are simpler:

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n - 1) z ^ {- n} = x (- 1) z ^ {0} + z ^ {- 1} \hat {X} (z) = z ^ {- 1} \hat {X} (z)
$$

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n - 2) z ^ {- n} = x (- 2) z ^ {0} + x (- 1) z ^ {- 1} + z ^ {- 2} \hat {X} (z) = z ^ {- 2} \hat {X} (z)
$$

$$
\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n - k) z ^ {- n} = x (- k) z ^ {0} + \dots + x (- 1) z ^ {- (k - 1)} + z ^ {- k} \hat {X} (z) = z ^ {- k} \hat {X} (z).
$$

(If there were non-zero initial conditions for $x(-1),\cdots,x(-k)$ ,we could include them in the Z transforms of $x(n-1)u(n),\cdots,x(n-k)u(n).$ ) Substituting these relations in (13.23) yields
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {Y} (z) + a _ {1} \left[ z ^ {- 1} \hat {Y} (z) + \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {0} \right] \\ + \dots \\ + a _ {m} \left[ z ^ {- m} \hat {Y} (z) + \bar {y} (- m) z ^ {0} + \dots \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- (m - 1)} \right] \\ = b _ {0} \hat {X} (z) + b _ {1} z ^ {- 1} \hat {X} (z) + \dots b _ {k} \hat {X} z ^ {- k}, \\ \end{array}
$$

(13.24)

from which, by rearranging terms, we obtain

$$
[ 1 + a _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \dots + a _ {m} z ^ {- m} ] \hat {Y} (z) = [ b _ {0} + b _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \dots + b _ {k} z ^ {- k} ] \hat {X} (z) + \hat {C} (z),
$$

where $\hat{C} (z)$ is an expression involving only the initial conditions

$$
\bar {y} (- 1), \dots , \bar {y} (- m).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Therefore,

$$
\hat {Y} (z) = \frac {b _ {0} + b _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \cdots b _ {k} z ^ {- k}}{1 + a _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \cdots + a _ {m} z ^ {- m}} \hat {X} (z) + \frac {\hat {C} (z)}{1 + a _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \cdots + a _ {m} z ^ {- m}}.
$$

We rewrite this relation as

$$
\hat {Y} (z) = \hat {H} (z) \hat {X} (z) + \frac {\hat {C} (z)}{1 + a _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \cdots + a _ {m} z ^ {- m}}.
$$

(13.25)

where

$$
\hat {H} (z) = \frac {b _ {0} + b _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \cdots + b _ {k} z ^ {- k}}{1 + a _ {1} z ^ {- 1} + \cdots + a _ {m} z ^ {- m}}.
$$

(13.26)

Observe that if the initial conditions are all zero, $\hat{C} (z)=0$ , and we only have the first term on the right in (13.25); and if the input is zero—i.e., $x(n)=0$ for all n, then $\hat{X} (z)=0$ , and we only have the second term.

By definition, $\hat{Y} (z)$ is the Z transform of the causal signal $y(n)u(n), n \in\mathbb{Z}$ . So its $RoC= \left\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid|z|>|p|\right\}$ in which p is the pole of the right side of (13.25) with the largest magnitude. The inverse Z transform of $\hat{Y}$ can be expressed as
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
\forall n \geq 0, \quad y (n) = y _ {z s} (n) + y _ {z i} (n),
$$

where $y_{zs}(n)$ , the inverse Z transform of $\hat{H}\hat{X}$ , is the zero-state response, and $y_{zi}(n)$ , the inverse Z transform of $\hat{C} (z) /[1+a_{1} z^{-1}+\cdots+a_{m} z^{-m}]$ , is the zero-input response. The zero-state response, also called the forced response, is the output when all initial conditions are zero. The zero-input response, also called the natural response, is the output when the input is zero.

Thus the (total) response is the sum of the zero-state and zero-input response. We first encountered this property of linearity in Chapter 5.

By definition, the transfer function is the Z transform of the zero-state impulse response. Taking $\hat{C}=0$ and $\hat{X}=1$ in (13.25) shows that the transfer function is $\hat{H} (z).$ From (13.26) we see that $\hat{H}$ can be written down by inspection of the difference equation (13.21). If the system is stable—all poles of $\hat{H}$ are inside the unit circle—the frequency response is

$$
\forall \omega , \quad H (\omega) = \hat {H} \left(e ^ {i \omega}\right) = \frac {b _ {0} + b _ {1} e ^ {- i \omega} + \cdots + b _ {k} e ^ {- i k \omega}}{1 + a _ {1} e ^ {- i \omega} + \cdots + a _ {m} e ^ {- i m \omega}}.
$$

We saw this relation in (8.21).
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Example 13.20: Consider the difference equation

$$
y (n) - \frac {5}{6} y (n - 1) + \frac {1}{6} y (n - 2) = x (n), n \geq 0.
$$

Taking Z transforms as in (13.24) yields

$$
\hat {Y} (z) - \frac {5}{6} \left[ z ^ {- 1} \hat {Y} (z) + \bar {y} (- 1) \right] + \frac {1}{6} \left[ z ^ {- 2} \hat {Y} (z) + \bar {y} (- 2) + \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- 1} \right] = \hat {X} (z).
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {Y} (z) = \frac {1}{1 - \frac {5}{6} z ^ {- 1} + \frac {1}{6} z ^ {- 2}} \hat {X} (z) + \frac {\frac {5}{6} \bar {y} (- 1) + \frac {1}{6} \bar {y} (- 2) + \frac {1}{6} \bar {y} (- 1) z ^ {- 1}}{1 - \frac {5}{6} z ^ {- 1} + \frac {1}{6} z ^ {- 2}} \\ = \frac {z ^ {2}}{z ^ {2} - \frac {5}{6} z + \frac {1}{6}} \hat {X} (z) + \frac {\left[ \frac {5}{6} \bar {y} (- 1) + \frac {1}{6} \bar {y} (- 2) \right] z ^ {2} + \frac {1}{6} \bar {y} (- 1) z}{z ^ {2} - \frac {5}{6} z + \frac {1}{6}}, \\ \end{array}
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
from which we can obtain $\hat{Y}$ for a specified $\hat{X}$ and initial conditions $\bar{y} (-1),\bar{y} (-2).$ The transfer function is

$$
\hat {H} (z) = \frac {z ^ {2}}{z ^ {2} - \frac {5}{6} z + \frac {1}{6}} = \frac {z ^ {2}}{(z - \frac {1}{3}) (z - \frac {1}{2})},
$$

which has poles at $z=1/3$ and $z=1/2$ (and two zeros at $z=0$ ). The system is stable. The zero-state impulse response $h$ is the inverse Z transform of $\hat{H} (z)$ , which we obtain using partial fraction expansion,

$$
\hat {H} (z) = z \left[ \frac {- 2}{z - \frac {1}{3}} + \frac {3}{z - \frac {1}{2}} \right]
$$

so that

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad h (n) = - 2 \left(\frac {1}{3}\right) ^ {n} u (n) + 3 \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) ^ {n} u (n).
$$

We can recognize that the impulse response consists of two terms, each contributed by one pole of the transfer function.

Suppose the initial conditions are $\bar{y}(-1)=1, \bar{y}(-2)=1$ and the input x is the unit step, so $\hat{X} ( z )=z /( z-1)$ . Then the zero-input response, $y_{zi}$ , has Z transform
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems
Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
SO

$$
\forall n, \quad y _ {z i} (n) = - 3 \left(\frac {1}{3}\right) ^ {n} u (n) + 4 \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) ^ {n} u (n).
$$

The zero-state response, $y_{zs}$ ,has Z transform

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {Y} _ {z s} (z) = \hat {H} (z) \hat {X} (z) = \frac {z ^ {3}}{(z - \frac {1}{3}) (z - \frac {1}{2}) (z - 1)} \\ = z \left[ \frac {1}{z - \frac {1}{3}} + \frac {- 3}{z - \frac {1}{2}} + \frac {3}{z - 1} \right], \\ \end{array}
$$

SO

$$
\forall n, \quad y _ {z s} (n) = \left(\frac {1}{3}\right) ^ {n} u (n) - 3 \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) ^ {n} u (n) + 3 u (n).
$$

The (total) response

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad y (n) = y _ {z s} (n) + y _ {z i} (n) = 3 u (n) + [ - 2 (1 / 3) ^ {n} + (1 / 2) ^ {n} ] u (n),
$$

can also be expressed as the sum of the steady-state and the transient response with $y_{ss}(n)=3 u(n)$ and $y_{tr}(n)=-2(1/3)^{n} u(n)+(1/2)^{n} u(n).$ Note that the decomposition of the response into the sum of the zero-state and zero-input responses is different from its decomposition into the steady-state and transient responses.

## 13.7.1 LTI differential equations

The analogous development for continuous time concerns systems described by a LTI differential equation of the form
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
## 13.7.1 LTI differential equations

The analogous development for continuous time concerns systems described by a LTI differential equation of the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {d ^ {m} y}{d t ^ {m}} (t) + a _ {m - 1} \frac {d ^ {m - 1} y}{d t ^ {m - 1}} (t) + \dots + a _ {1} \frac {d y}{d t} (t) + a _ {0} y (t) \\ = b _ {k} \frac {d ^ {k} x}{d t ^ {k}} (t) + \dots + b _ {1} \frac {d x}{d t} (t) + b _ {0} x (t), t \geq 0. \\ \end{array}
$$

(13.27)

We interpret this equation as describing a causal continuous-time LTI system in which $x(t)$ is the input and $y(t)$ is the output at time t. The constant coefficients $a_{i}$ and $b_{j}$ specify the system.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
In section 8.2.1 we used this form to find the frequency response. In example 13.11, we used the Laplace transform to find the transfer function of a tuning force. But in both cases, we assumed that the system was initially at rest. We now develop a method to find the response to arbitrary initial conditions. We begin with a simple circuit example.

Example 13.21: A series connection of a resistor R, a capacitor C, and a voltage source x, is described by the differential equation

$$
\frac {d y}{d t} (t) + \frac {1}{R C} y (t) = x (t),
$$

in which $y$ is the voltage across the capacitor. The differential equation is obtained from Kirchhoff's voltage law. The transfer function of this system is $\hat{H} (s) = 1 / (s+ 1 / RC).$ So if the system is initially at rest, we can calculate the response y from its Laplace transform $\hat{Y} = \hat{H}\hat{X}.$ For instance, if the input is a unit step, $\hat{X} (s) = 1 / s,$

$$
\hat {Y} (s) = \frac {1}{(s + 1 / R C) s} = \frac {- R C}{s + 1 / R C} + \frac {R C}{s},
$$

therefore, $y(t) = -R C e^{-t / R C} + R C, t \geq 0.$

We cannot use this transfer function, however, to determine the response if the initial capacitor voltage is $y ( 0 )=\bar{y} ( 0 )$ and $x ( t )=0, t\geq0.$ The response in this case is

$$
y (t) = \bar {y} (0) e ^ {- t / R C}, t \geq 0.
$$

We can check that expression is correct by verifying that it satisfies the given initial condition and the differential equation.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
y (t) = \bar {y} (0) e ^ {- t / R C}, t \geq 0.
$$

We can check that expression is correct by verifying that it satisfies the given initial condition and the differential equation.

If the initial condition is $y ( 0 )=\bar{y} ( 0 )$ and the input is a unit step, the response turns out to be the sum of the response due to the input (with zero initial condition) and the response due to the initial condition (with zero input),

$$
y (t) = \left[ - R C e ^ {- t / R C} + R C \right] + \left[ \bar {y} (0) e ^ {- t / R C} \right], t \geq 0.
$$

For the general case (13.27) we assume that the input $x$ starts at some finite time which we take to be zero, so $x ( t )=0,t<0.$ We wish to calculate $y ( t ),t\geq 0.$ From the theory of
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
differential equations we know that we need to be given m initial conditions,

$$
y (0) = \bar {y} (0), \frac {d y}{d t} (0) = \bar {y} ^ {(1)} (0), \dots , \frac {d ^ {m - 1} y}{d t ^ {m - 1}} (0) = \bar {y} ^ {(m - 1)} (0),
$$

in order to calculate $y ( t ) , t \geq 0 .$

Because time is continuous, there is no recursive procedure for calculating the output from the given data as we did in (13.22). Instead we calculate the output signal using the Laplace transform. We define the Laplace transforms of the signals $y ( t ) u ( t ) , y ^ { ( 1 ) } ( t ) u ( t ) , \cdots , y ^ { ( m ) } ($

$$
\hat {Y} (s) = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} y (t) u (t) e ^ {- s t} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} y (t) e ^ {- s t} d t
$$

$$
\hat {Y} ^ {(i)} (s) = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} y ^ {(i)} (t) u (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} y ^ {(i)} (t) e ^ {- s t} d t, i = 1, \dots , m
$$

$$
\hat {X} (s) = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} x (t) u (t) e ^ {- s t} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} x (t) e ^ {- s t} d t.
$$

Here we use the notation $y^{(i)}(t)=\frac{d^{i} t}{d t^{i}} y(t), t \geq 0$ . We now derive the relations between these Laplace transforms.

The derivative $y^{(1)}(t)=\frac{dy}{dt}(t)$ and y are related by
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
The derivative $y^{(1)}(t)=\frac{dy}{dt}(t)$ and y are related by

$$
y (t) u (t) = y (0) u (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} y ^ {(1)} (\tau) u (\tau) d \tau = \bar {y} (0) u (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} y ^ {(1)} (\tau) u (\tau) d \tau , t \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Using integration by parts,

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {Y} (s) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} y (t) e ^ {- s t} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \bar {y} (0) e ^ {- s t} d t + \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \left(\int_ {0} ^ {t} y ^ {(1)} (\tau) d \tau\right) e ^ {- s t} d t \\ = \frac {1}{s} \bar {y} (0) - \frac {1}{s} \int_ {0} ^ {t} y ^ {(1)} (\tau) d \tau e ^ {- s t} | _ {t = 0} ^ {\infty} + \frac {1}{s} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} y ^ {(1)} (t) e ^ {- s t} d t \\ = \frac {1}{s} [ \hat {Y} ^ {(1)} (s) + \bar {y} (0) ]. \\ \end{array}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed {\hat {Y} ^ {(1)} (s) = s \hat {Y} (s) - \bar {y} (0).}
$$

(13.28)

Repeating this procedure, we get the Laplace transforms of the higher-order derivatives,
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
\boxed {\hat {Y} ^ {(1)} (s) = s \hat {Y} (s) - \bar {y} (0).}
$$

(13.28)

Repeating this procedure, we get the Laplace transforms of the higher-order derivatives,

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {Y} ^ {(2)} (s) = s \hat {Y} ^ {(1)} (s) - \bar {y} ^ {(1)} (0) \\ = s ^ {2} \hat {Y} (s) - s \bar {y} (0) - \bar {y} ^ {(1)} (0) \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\hat {Y} ^ {(m)} (s) = s ^ {m} \hat {Y} (s) - s ^ {m - 1} \bar {y} (0) - s ^ {m - 2} \bar {y} ^ {(1)} (0) - \dots - \bar {y} ^ {(m - 1)} (0).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
On the other hand, because $x^{(i)}(t)=\frac{d^{i}x}{dt^{i}}(t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ , using the differentiation property in table 13.4, we obtain

$$
\hat {X} ^ {(1)} (s) = s \hat {X} (s)
$$

$$
\hat {X} ^ {(k)} (s) = s ^ {k} \hat {X} (s).
$$

By substituting from the relations just derived, we obtain the Laplace transforms of all the terms in (13.27),

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left[ s ^ {m} \hat {Y} (s) - s ^ {m - 1} \bar {y} (0) - \dots - \bar {y} ^ {m - 1} (0) \right] \\ + a _ {m - 1} \left[ s ^ {m - 1} \hat {Y} (s) - s ^ {m - 2} \bar {y} (0) - \dots - \bar {y} ^ {m - 2} (0) \right] \\ \dots \\ + a _ {1} \left[ s \hat {Y} (s) - \bar {y} (0) \right] \\ + a _ {0} \hat {Y} (s) \\ = b _ {k} s ^ {k} \hat {X} (s) + \dots + b _ {1} s \hat {X} (s) + b _ {0} \hat {X} (s). \\ \end{array}
$$

(13.29)

Rearranging terms yields

$$
\left[ s ^ {m} + a _ {m - 1} s ^ {m - 1} + \dots + a _ {1} s + a _ {0} \right] \hat {Y} (s) = \left[ b _ {k} s ^ {k} + \dots + b _ {1} s + b _ {0} \right] \hat {X} (s) + \hat {C} (s),
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
in which $\hat{C}$ is an expression involving only the initial conditions

$$
\bar {y} (0), \dots , \bar {y} ^ {(m - 1)} (0).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\hat {Y} (s) = \frac {b _ {k} s ^ {k} + b _ {k - 1} s ^ {k - 1} + \cdots b _ {1} s + b _ {0}}{s ^ {m} + a _ {m - 1} s ^ {m - 1} + \cdots a _ {1} s + a _ {0}} \hat {X} (s) + \frac {\hat {C} (s)}{s ^ {m} + a _ {m - 1} s ^ {m - 1} + \cdots a _ {1} s + a _ {0}},
$$

(13.30)

which we also write as

$$
\hat {Y} (s) = \hat {H} (s) \hat {X} (s) + \frac {\hat {C} (s)}{s ^ {m} + a _ {m - 1} s ^ {m - 1} + \cdots a _ {1} s + a _ {0}},
$$

(13.31)

in which

$$
\hat {H} (s) = \frac {b _ {k} s ^ {k} + \cdots + b _ {1} s + b _ {0}}{s ^ {m} + \cdots + a _ {1} s + a _ {0}}.
$$

(13.32)
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
If the initial conditions are all zero, $\hat{C} (s)=0$ , and we only have the first term on the right in (13.31); if the input is zero—i.e., $x(t)=0$ for all t, then $\hat{X} (s)=0$ , and we only get the second term in (13.31).

By definition, $\hat{Y} (s)$ is the Laplace transform of the causal signal $y(t)u(t), t\in\mathbb{R}$ . So its $RoC=\{s\in\mathbb{C}\mid Re\{s\}>Re\{p\}\}$ , where p is a pole of the right side of (13.31) with the largest real part.

Taking the inverse Laplace transform of $\hat{Y}$ , we can decompose the output signal y as

$$
\forall t, \quad y (t) = y _ {z s} (t) + y _ {z i} (t),
$$

where $y_{zs}$ , the inverse Laplace transform of $\hat{H}\hat{X}$ , is the zero-state or forced response and $y_{zi}$ , the inverse Laplace transform of $\hat{C}(s) /[ s^{m}+\cdots+a_{0}]$ , is the zero-input or natural response. The (total) response is the sum of the zero-state and zero-input response, which is a general property of linear systems.

By definition, the transfer function is the Laplace transform of the zero-state impulse response. Taking $\hat{C}=0$ and $\hat{X}=1$ (the Laplace transform of the unit impulse) in (13.31) shows that the transfer function is $\hat{H} (s)$ which, as we see from (13.32), can be written down by inspection of the differential equation (13.27). If the system is stable—all poles of $\hat{H} (s)$ have real parts strictly less than zero—the frequency response is, as in (8.23)
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
\forall \omega , \quad H (\omega) = \hat {H} (i \omega) = \frac {b _ {k} (i \omega) ^ {k} + \cdots + b _ {1} i \omega + b _ {0}}{(i \omega) ^ {m} + \cdots + a _ {1} i \omega + a _ {0}}.
$$

Example 13.22: We find the response $y ( t ) , t \geq 0$ , for the differential equation

$$
\frac {d ^ {2} y}{d t ^ {2}} + 3 \frac {d y}{d t} + 2 y = 3 x (t) + \frac {d x}{d t},
$$

when the input is a unit step $x(t)=u(t)$ and the initial conditions are $y(0)= 1, y^{(1)}(0)=2.$ Taking Laplace transforms of both sides as in (13.29),

$$
[ s ^ {2} \hat {Y} (s) - s \bar {y} (0) - \bar {y} ^ {(1)} (0) ] + 3 [ s \hat {Y} (s) - \bar {y} (0) ] + 2 \hat {Y} (s) = 3 \hat {X} (s) + s \hat {X} (s).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\hat {Y} (s) = \frac {s + 3}{s ^ {2} + 3 s + 2} \hat {X} (s) + \frac {s \bar {y} (0) + \bar {y} ^ {(1)} (0) + 3 \bar {y} (0)}{s ^ {2} + 3 s + 2}.
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Substituting $\hat{X} (s)=1 / s,\bar{y} (0)=1, \bar{y}^{(1)}=2$ , yields

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {Y} (s) = \frac {s + 3}{s \left(s ^ {2} + 3 s + 2\right)} + \frac {s + 5}{s ^ {2} + 3 s + 2} \\ = \left[ \frac {3 / 2}{s} - \frac {2}{s + 1} + \frac {1 / 2}{s + 2} \right] + \left[ \frac {4}{s + 1} - \frac {3}{s + 2} \right]. \\ \end{array}
$$

Taking inverse Laplace transforms gives

$$
\begin{array}{l} \forall t, y (t) = y _ {z s} (t) + y _ {z i} (t) \\ = \left[ \frac {3}{2} u (t) - 2 e ^ {- t} u (t) + \frac {1}{2} e ^ {- 2 t} u (t) \right] + \left[ 4 e ^ {- t} u (t) - 3 e ^ {- 2 t} u (t) \right] \\ = \frac {3}{2} u (t) + \left[ 2 e ^ {- t} - \frac {5}{2} e ^ {- 2 t} \right] u (t) \\ = y _ {s s} (t) + y _ {t r} (t). \\ \end{array}
$$

As in the case of difference equations, the decomposition of the response into zero-state and zero-input responses is different from the decomposition into transient and steady-state responses. (Indeed, the steady-state response does not exist if the system is unstable, whereas the former decomposition always exists.)

## 13.8 State-space models

This section is mathematically more advanced in that it uses the operation of matrix inverse.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
## 13.8 State-space models

This section is mathematically more advanced in that it uses the operation of matrix inverse.

In section 5.3 we introduced single-input, single-output (SISO) multidimensional state-space models of discrete-time and continuous-time LTI systems. For LTI systems, state-space models provide an alternative description to difference or differential equation representations. The advantage of state-space models is that by using matrix notation we have a very compact representation of the response, independent of the order of the system. We develop a method that combines this matrix notation with transform techniques to calculate the response.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
The discrete-time SISO state-space model is

$$
\forall n \geq 0, \quad s (n + 1) = A s (n) + b x (n),
$$

(13.33)

$$
y (n) = c ^ {T} s (n) + d x (n),
$$

(13.34)

in which $s(n)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ is the state, $x(n)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the input, and $y(n)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the output at time n. In this $[A,b,c,d]$ representation, A is an $N\times N$ (square) matrix, b,c are N-dimensional column vectors, and d is a scalar. If the initial state is $s(0)$ , and the input sequence is $x(0),x(1),\cdots$ , by recursively using (13.33) and (13.34) we obtain the state and output responses:

$$
s (n) = A ^ {n} s (0) + \sum_ {m = 0} ^ {n - 1} A ^ {n - 1 - m} b x (m),
$$

(13.35)

$$
y (n) = c ^ {T} A ^ {n} s (0) + \left\{\sum_ {m = 0} ^ {n - 1} c ^ {T} A ^ {n - 1 - m} b x (m) + d x (n) \right\},
$$

(13.36)

for all n $\geq 0$ . Notice that these "closed-form" formulas for the response are independent of the order N. Difference equation representations do not have such a closed-form formula.

Example 13.23: Consider the system described by the difference equation

$$
y (n) - 2 y (n - 1) - 3 y (n - 2) = x (n).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Example 13.23: Consider the system described by the difference equation

$$
y (n) - 2 y (n - 1) - 3 y (n - 2) = x (n).
$$

As in section 5.3, we can construct a state-space model for this system by noting that the state at time n should remember the previous two inputs y(n-1),y(n-2). Define the two-dimensional state vector $s ( n )=\left[ s_{1} ( n ) \, s_{2} ( n ) \right]^{T}$ by $s_{1}(n)=y(n- 1),s_{2}(n)=ay(n-2)$ , in which a $\neq0$ is a constant. Problem 23 at the end of this chapter asks you to show that the $[ A,b,c,d]$ representation for this choice of state is given by

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 2 & 3 / a \\ a & 0 \end{array} \right], \quad b = \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right], \quad c ^ {T} = [ 2 \quad 3 / a ], \text {a n d} d = 1.
$$

Different choices of a give a different state-space model. However, they all have the same input-output relation because they all have the same transfer function.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
We will obtain the Z transforms of the response sequences (13.35),(13.36). The key is to compute the Z transform of the entire $N\times N$ matrix sequence $A^{n}u(n), n\in\mathbb{Z}.$ This Z transform is

$$
\boxed {\sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} z ^ {- n} A ^ {n} = \left[ I - z ^ {- 1} A \right] ^ {- 1} = z \left[ z I - A \right] ^ {- 1}.}
$$

(13.37)

Here z is a complex number and I is the $N\times N$ identity matrix. The series on the left is an infinite sum of $N\times N$ matrices which converges to the $N\times N$ matrix on the right, for $z\in RoC. RoC$ is determined later.

Assuming the series converges, it is easy to check the equality (13.37): Just multiply both sides by $[ I-z^{-1} A ]$ and verify that

$$
[ I - z ^ {- 1} A ] \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} z ^ {- n} A ^ {n} = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} z ^ {- n} A ^ {- n} - \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} z ^ {- (n + 1)} A ^ {n + 1} = z ^ {0} A ^ {0} = I.
$$

Next, denote by F the matrix inverse,

$$
F (z) = \left[ I - z ^ {- 1} A \right] ^ {- 1} = z \left[ z I - A \right] ^ {- 1},
$$

(13.38)

and the coefficients of $A^{n}$ and F(z) by

$$
A ^ {n} = \left[ a _ {i j} (n) \mid 1 \leq i, j \leq N \right], \quad F (z) = \left[ f _ {i j} (z) \mid 1 \leq i, j \leq N \right].
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Then $f_{ij}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^{-n} a_{ij}(n)$ is the Z transform of the sequence $a_{ij}(n), n\geq 0, 1\leq i,j\leq N.$ So we can obtain $A^{n}, n\geq 0,$ by taking the inverse Z transform of each of the $N^{2}$ coefficients of F(z).

Example 13.24: Let

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{array} \right],
$$

then

$$
[ z I - A ] ^ {- 1} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} z - 2 & - 1 \\ - 3 & z - 4 \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{\det [ z I - A ]} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} z - 4 & 1 \\ 3 & z - 2 \end{array} \right],
$$

in which det $[zI-A]$ denotes the determinant of $[zI-A]$

$$
\det [ z I - A ] = (z - 2) (z - 4) - 3 = z ^ {2} - 6 z + 5 = (z - 1) (z - 5).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Hence,

$$
\begin{array}{l} F (z) = z [ z I - A ] ^ {- 1} = \frac {z}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} z - 4 & 1 \\ 3 & z - 2 \end{array} \right] \\ = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {z (z - 4)}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} & \frac {z}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \\ \frac {3 z}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} & \frac {z (z - 2)}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \end{array} \right]. \\ \end{array}
$$

The partial fraction expansion of the coefficients of F is

$$
F (z) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {(3 / 4) z}{z - 1} + \frac {(1 / 4) z}{z - 5} & \frac {(- 1 / 4) z}{z - 1} + \frac {(1 / 4) z}{z - 5} \\ \frac {(- 3 / 4) z}{z - 1} + \frac {(3 / 4) z}{z - 5} & \frac {(1 / 4) z}{z - 1} + \frac {(3 / 4) z}{z - 5} \end{array} \right].
$$

Using table 13.1 we find the inverse Z transform of every coefficient of $F ( z )$ : for all n $\in\mathbb{Z}$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Using table 13.1 we find the inverse Z transform of every coefficient of $F ( z )$ : for all n $\in\mathbb{Z}$

$$
A ^ {n} u (n) = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {3}{4} u (n) + \frac {1}{4} 5 ^ {n} u (n) & - \frac {1}{4} u (n) + \frac {1}{4} 5 ^ {n} u (n) \\ - \frac {3}{4} u (n) + \frac {3}{4} 5 ^ {n} u (n) & \frac {1}{4} u (n) + \frac {3}{4} 5 ^ {n} u (n) \end{array} \right].
$$

This is more revealingly expressed as

$$
A ^ {n} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 3 / 4 & - 1 / 4 \\ - 3 / 4 & 1 / 4 \end{array} \right] + 5 ^ {n} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 / 4 & 1 / 4 \\ 3 / 4 & 3 / 4 \end{array} \right], \quad n \geq 0,
$$

because it shows that the variation in n of $A^{n}$ is determined by the two poles, at $z=1$ and $z=5$ , in the coefficients of F(z). Moreover, these two poles are the zeros of

$$
\det [ z I - A ] = (z - 1) (z - 5).
$$

This determinant is called the characteristic polynomial of the matrix A and its zeros are called the eigenvalues of A. The domain of convergence is $R o C=\{z\in \mathbb{C} \mid |z|>5\}.$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
We return to the general case in (13.38). Denote the matrix inverse of $[zI - A]$ as

$$
[ z I - A ] ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{\det [ z I - A ]} G (z),
$$

in which $G ( z )$ is the $N \times N$ matrix of co-factors of $[ z I-A ]$ . It follows that each coefficient $f_{ij} ( z )$ of $F ( z )=z[ z I-A ]^{-1}$ is a rational polynomial whose denominator is the characteristic polynomial of A, $\det[ z I-A ]$ . Therefore, if there are no pole-zero cancellations, all coefficients of F(z) have the same poles, which are the zeros of $\det[ z I-A ]$ . These zeros are called the eigenvalues of A. The polynomial $\det[ z I-A ]$ is of order N, and so A has N eigenvalues.

Because $A^{n}u(n), n\in\mathbb{Z},$ is a causal sequence, the region of convergence is $RoC=\{z\in \mathbb{C}||z|>|p|\},$ in which p is the pole of F (or eigenvalue of A) with the largest magnitude. For the system (13.33), (13.34) to be stable, the poles of F must have magnitudes strictly smaller than 1.

Suppose $A$ has $N$ distinct eigenvalues $p_{1},\dots,p_{N}$

$$
\det [ z I - A ] = \left(z - p _ {1}\right) \dots \left(z - p _ {N}\right).
$$

Then the partial fraction expansion of F(z) has the form

$$
F (z) = \frac {z}{z - p _ {1}} R _ {1} + \dots + \frac {z}{z - p _ {N}} R _ {N},
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Then the partial fraction expansion of F(z) has the form

$$
F (z) = \frac {z}{z - p _ {1}} R _ {1} + \dots + \frac {z}{z - p _ {N}} R _ {N},
$$

in which $R_{i}$ is the matrix of residues of the coefficients of F at the pole $p_{i}.$ $R_{i}$ is a constant matrix, possibly with complex coefficients if $p_{i}$ is complex. Recalling that $\frac{z}{z-p_{i}}$ is the inverse Z transform of $p_{i}^{n} u(n)$ , we can take the inverse Z transform of F(z) to conclude that

$$
\boxed {A ^ {n} = p _ {1} ^ {n} R _ {1} + \dots p _ {N} ^ {n} R _ {N}, \quad n \geq 0.}
$$

(13.39)

Thus $A^{n}$ is a linear combination of $p_{1}^{n},\cdots,p_{N}^{n}.$

We can decompose the response (13.36) into the zero-input and zero-state responses, expressing the latter as a convolution sum,

$$
y (n) = c ^ {T} A ^ {n} s (0) + \sum_ {m = 0} ^ {n} h (n - m) x (m), n \geq 0,
$$

where the (zero-state) impulse response is

$$
h (n) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & n < 0 \\ d, & n = 0 \\ c ^ {T} A ^ {n - 1} b, & n \geq 1 \end{array} . \right.
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Let $\hat{X},\hat{Y},\hat{H},\hat{Y}_{zi}$ be the Z transforms:

$$
\hat {X} (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} x (n) z ^ {- n}, \quad \hat {Y} (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} y (n) z ^ {- n},
$$

$$
\hat {H} (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} h (n) z ^ {- n}, \quad \hat {Y} _ {z i} (z) = \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {\infty} c ^ {T} z ^ {- n} A ^ {n} s (0).
$$

Then

$$
\hat {Y} = \hat {H} \hat {X} + \hat {Y} _ {z i}.
$$

Because $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^{-n} A^{n}=z[z I-A]^{-1}$ , we obtain

$$
\hat {H} (z) = c ^ {T} [ z I - A ] ^ {- 1} b + d,
$$

and

$$
\hat {Y} _ {z i} (z) = z c ^ {T} [ z I - A ] ^ {- 1} s (0).
$$

Example 13.25: Suppose A is as in example 13.24, $b^{T}=[1\ 1], c^{T}=[2\ 0], d=3$ and $( s(0))^{T}=[0\ 4]$. Then the transfer function is

$$
\hat {H} (z) = [ 2 0 ] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {(z - 4)}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} & \frac {1}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \\ \frac {3}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} & \frac {(z - 2)}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right] + 3 = \frac {2 (z - 4) + 2}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} + 3,
$$

and the Z transform of the zero-input response is

$$
\hat {Y} _ {z i} (z) = [ 2 0 ] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {z (z - 4)}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} & \frac {z}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \\ \frac {3 z}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} & \frac {z (z - 2)}{(z - 1) (z - 5)} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 4 \end{array} \right] = \frac {8 z}{(z - 1) (z - 5)}.
$$

The transfer function

text:
From (13.26) we recognize that $\hat{H}$ is also the transfer function of the difference equation

$$
y (n) - 6 y (n - 1) + 5 y (n - 2) = 3 x (n) - 1 6 x (n - 1) + 9 x (n - 2).

This difference equation describes the same input-output relation as the state-space model of this example.

## 13.8.1 Continuous-time state-space models

The continuous-time SISO state-space model introduced in section 5.4 has the representation in terms of $[ A,b,c,d]$

$$
\dot {v} (t) = A v (t) + b x (t),
$$

(13.40)

$$
y (t) = c ^ {T} v (t) + d x (t),
$$

(13.41)

in which $\nu(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ is the state, $x(t)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the input, and $y(t)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the output at time $t\in\mathbb{R}.$ A is an $N\times N$ matrix, and b,c are N-dimensional column vectors, and d is a scalar. (We use $\nu$ instead of s to denote the state, because s is reserved for the Laplace transform variable.)

Given the initial state $\nu(0)$ and the input signal $x(t), t\geq 0$ , we will show that the state response and the output response obey the formulas

$$
v (t) = e ^ {t A} v (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {(t - \tau) A} b x (\tau) d \tau ,
$$

(13.42)

$$
y (t) = c ^ {T} e ^ {t A} v (0) + \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {t} c ^ {T} e ^ {(t - \tau) A} b x (\tau) d \tau \right] + d x (t).
$$

(13.43)
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
(13.43)

In these formulas, $e^{tA}$ or $\exp(t A)$ is the name of the $N\times N$ matrix

$$
e ^ {t A} = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {(t A) ^ {k}}{k !} = I + t A + \frac {(t A) ^ {2}}{2 !} + \frac {(t A) ^ {3}}{3 !} + \dots ,
$$

(13.44)

where $( t A )^{k}$ is the matrix $t A$ multiplied by itself k times, and $( t A )^{0}=I$ , the $N\times N$ identity matrix. Definition (13.44) of the matrix exponential is the natural generalization of the exponential of a real or complex number. (The series in (13.44) is absolutely summable because of the factor k! in the denominator.)
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Unlike in the discrete-time case, there is no recursive procedure to compute the responses (13.42), (13.43). This is because time is continuous, and the difficulty has to do with the integrals in these formulas. For numerical calculation, one resorts to a finite sum approximation of the integrals, as we indicated in Section 5.4. The Laplace transform provides an alternative approach that is exact.

The key to showing (13.42) is the fact that $e^{t A}, t \geq 0$ , is the solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac {d}{d t} e ^ {t A} = A e ^ {t A}, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

(13.45)

with initial condition $e^{0 A}=I$ . Note that (13.43) follows immediately from (13.42) and (13.41).

To verify (13.45) we substitute for $e^{t A}$ from (13.44) and differentiate the sum term by term,

$$
\frac {d}{d t} e ^ {t A} = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {\infty} \frac {d}{d t} \frac {(t A) ^ {k}}{k !} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {k A}{k !} (t A) ^ {k - 1} = A \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {\infty} \frac {(t A) ^ {k - 1}}{(k - 1) !} = A e ^ {t A}.
$$

We can now check that (13.42) is indeed the solution of (13.40) by taking derivatives of both sides and using (13.45):
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
We can now check that (13.42) is indeed the solution of (13.40) by taking derivatives of both sides and using (13.45):

$$
\begin{array}{l} \dot {v} (t) = A e ^ {t A} v (0) + e ^ {0 A} b x (t) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} A e ^ {(t - \tau) A} b x (\tau) d \tau \\ = A \left[ e ^ {t A} v (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} A e ^ {(t - \tau) A} b x (\tau) d \tau \right] + b x (t) \\ = A v (t) + b x (t). \\ \end{array}
$$

We turn to the main difficulty in calculating the terms on the right in the responses (13.42), (13.43), namely the calculation of the $N\times N$ matrix $e^{t A}, t\geq 0.$ We determine the Laplace transform of $e^{t A} u ( t ), t\in \mathbb{R},$ denoting it by

$$
G (s) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {t A} e ^ {- s t} d t.
$$

This means that $g_{ij}(s)$ is the Laplace transform of $a_{ij}(t), t\geq 0$ , denoting by $a_{ij}(t)$ and $g_{ij}(s)$ the coefficients of the $N\times N$ matrices $e^{tA}$ and G(s), respectively. The region of convergence of G, RoC, is determined later.

Using the derivative formula (13.28) in (13.45) we see that

$$
s G (s) - I = A G (s),
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
which gives $G(s)=[s I-A]^{-1}$ , so that the Laplace transform of $e^{t A} u(t)$ is

$$
\boxed {G (s) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {t A} e ^ {- s t} d t = [ s I - A ] ^ {- 1}.}
$$

(13.46)

Example 13.26: Let

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 & 2 \\ - 2 & 1 \end{array} \right],
$$

then

$$
[ s I - A ] ^ {- 1} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} s - 1 & - 2 \\ 2 & s - 1 \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{\det [ s I - A ]} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} s - 1 & 2 \\ - 2 & s - 1 \end{array} \right].
$$

The determinant is

$$
\det [ s I - A ] = (s - 1) ^ {2} + 4 = (s - 1 + 2 i) (s - 1 - 2 i),
$$

so that
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
The determinant is

$$
\det [ s I - A ] = (s - 1) ^ {2} + 4 = (s - 1 + 2 i) (s - 1 - 2 i),
$$

so that

$$
\begin{array}{l} [ s I - A ] ^ {- 1} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {s - 1}{(s - 1 + 2 i) (s - 1 - 2 i)} & \frac {2}{(s - 1 + 2 i) (s - 1 - 2 i)} \\ \frac {- 2}{(s - 1 + 2 i) (s - 1 - 2 i)} & \frac {s - 1}{(s - 1 + 2 i) (s - 1 - 2 i)} \end{array} \right] \\ = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1 / 2}{s - 1 + 2 i} + \frac {1 / 2}{s - 1 - 2 i} & \frac {i / 2}{s - 1 + 2 i} + \frac {- i / 2}{s - 1 - 2 i} \\ \frac {- i / 2}{s - 1 + 2 i} + \frac {i / 2}{s - 1 - 2 i} & \frac {1 / 2}{s - 1 + 2 i} + \frac {1 / 2}{s - 1 - 2 i} \end{array} \right]. \\ \end{array}
$$

The region of convergence $R o C=\{s\in \mathbb{C}\mid Re\{s\}>1\}$ . We find the inverse Laplace transform using table 13.3 and express it in two ways: for all $t\geq0,$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
The region of convergence $R o C=\{s\in \mathbb{C}\mid Re\{s\}>1\}$ . We find the inverse Laplace transform using table 13.3 and express it in two ways: for all $t\geq0,$

$$
\begin{array}{l} e ^ {t A} = e ^ {(1 - 2 i) t} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 / 2 & i / 2 \\ - i / 2 & 1 / 2 \end{array} \right] + e ^ {(1 + 2 i) t} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 1 / 2 & - i / 2 \\ i / 2 & 1 / 2 \end{array} \right] \\ = e ^ {t} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \cos 2 t & \sin 2 t \\ - \sin 2 t & \cos 2 t \end{array} \right]. \\ \end{array}
$$

The first expression shows $e^{t A}$ as a linear combination of the exponentials $e^{(1-2 i) t}$ and $e^{(1+2 i) t}$ , in which the exponents, 1-2i and 1+2i, are the two eigenvalues of A—that is, the zeros of its characteristic polynomial, $\det[ s I-A]$ . The second expression shows that $e^{t A}$ is sinusoidal with frequency 2 radians/sec equal to the imaginary part of the eigenvalues whose amplitude grows exponentially corresponding to the real part of the eigenvalues.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Returning to the general case (13.46), denote the matrix inverse of $[ s I-A ]$ as

$$
G (s) = \left[ s I - A \right] ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{\det [ s I - A ]} K (s),
$$

in which $K(s)$ is the $N\times N$ matrix of co-factors of $[sI-A]$ . Each coefficient $g_{ij}(s)$ of $G(s)$ is a rational polynomial of A whose denominator is the characteristic polynomial of A, $\det[sI-A]$ . Therefore, if there are no pole-zero cancellations, all coefficients of $G(s)$ have the same poles—the eigenvalues of A. Because $e^{tA}u(t), t\in\mathbb{R}$ , is a causal signal, the region of convergence of its Laplace transform $G(s)$ is $\{s\in\mathbb{C}\mid Re\{s\}>Re\{p\} \}$ , in which p is the pole of G with the largest real part.

Because $\det[s I-A]$ is a polynomial of order N, G has N poles. For the system (13.40), (13.41) to be stable, the poles of $G(s)$ must have strictly negative real parts. The system of example (13.26) is unstable, because the real part of the eigenvalues is +1.

Suppose the characteristic polynomial has $N$ distinct zeros $p_{1},\dots,p_{N}$

$$
\det [ s I - A ] = \left(s - p _ {1}\right) \dots \left(s - p _ {N}\right).
$$

Then the partial fraction expansion of $G(s)$ has the form

$$
G (s) = \left[ s I - A \right] ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{s - p _ {1}} R _ {1} + \dots + \frac {1}{s - p _ {N}} R _ {N},
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
G (s) = \left[ s I - A \right] ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{s - p _ {1}} R _ {1} + \dots + \frac {1}{s - p _ {N}} R _ {N},
$$

in which $R_{i}$ is the matrix of residues at the pole $p_{i}$ of the coefficients of $G(s).$ $R_{i}$ is a constant matrix, possibly with complex coefficients, if $p_{i}$ is complex. Because the inverse Laplace transform of $\frac{1}{s-p_{i}}$ is $e^{p_{i} t} u(t)$ , the inverse Laplace transform of $[sI-A]^{-1}$ is

$$
\left| e ^ {t A} u (t) = \left[ e ^ {p _ {1} t} R _ {1} + \dots + e ^ {p _ {N} t} R _ {N} \right] u (t). \right|
$$

(13.47)

Thus the matrix $e^{t A}$ as a function of t is a linear combination of $e^{p_{1} t}, \cdots, e^{p_{N} t}$ , where the $p_{i}$ are the eigenvalues of A—that is the zeros of $\det[s I-A]$ .

We decompose the response (13.43) into the sum of the zero-input and zero-state responses, expressing the latter as a convolution integral,

$$
y (t) = c ^ {T} e ^ {t A} v (0) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} h (t - \tau) x (\tau) d \tau , t \geq 0,
$$

in which the (zero-state) impulse response is: for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$

$$
h (t) = c ^ {T} e ^ {t A} b u (t) + d \delta (t).
$$
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
(Here $\delta$ is the Dirac delta function.) Let $\hat{X},\hat{Y},\hat{H},\hat{Y}_{zi}$ be the Laplace transforms

$$
\hat {X} (s) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} x (t) e ^ {- s t} d t, \quad \hat {Y} (s) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} y (t) e ^ {- s t} d t,
$$

$$

Thus we can use any of three equivalent representations of LTI systems:

- difference or differential equations, used to describe many physical systems,

text:
## 13.9 Summary

The Z transform and Laplace transform have many of the same properties as the Fourier transforms. They are linear, which greatly facilitates computation of the transforms and their inverses. Moreover, the Z transform (Laplace transform) of the output of an LTI system is the product of the Z transforms (Laplace transforms) of the input and the transfer function. Thus, the Z transform (Laplace transform) plays the same role as the frequency response, describing the relationship between the input and the output as a product rather than a convolution.

Linear difference and differential equations, and state-space models of LTI systems were introduced in Chapter 5 and Chapter 8. However, we lacked a method to calculate the response of these models for non-zero initial conditions. The Z transform and the Laplace transform provide such a method.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
## Probing Further: Derivatives of Z transforms

Calculus on complex-valued functions of complex variables can be intricate. Suppose $\hat{X}$ is a function of a complex variable. The derivative can be defined as a limit,

$$
\frac {d}{d z} \hat {X} (z) = \lim _ {\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac {\hat {X} (z + \varepsilon) - \hat {X} (z)}{\varepsilon},
$$

where $\varepsilon$ is a complex variable that can approach zero from any direction in the complex plane. The derivative exists if the limit does not depend on the direction. If the derivative exists at all points within a distance $\varepsilon>0$ of a point z in the complex plane, then $\hat{X}$ is said to be analytic at z. A Z transform is a series of the form

$$
\forall z \in R o C (x), \quad \hat {X} (z) = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} x (n) z ^ {- n}.
$$

This is called a Laurent series in the theory of complex variables. It can be shown that a Laurent series is analytic at all points $z\in RoC(x)$ , and that the derivative is

$$
\forall z \in R o C (x), \quad \frac {d}{d z} \hat {X} (z) = \sum_ {m = - \infty} ^ {\infty} - m x (m) z ^ {- m - 1}.
$$

We can use this fact to show that the Z transform of y given by $y(n)=nx(n)$ is

$$
\forall z \in R o c (x), \quad \hat {Y} (z) = - z \frac {d}{d z} \hat {X} (z).
$$

This is because
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
$$
\forall z \in R o c (x), \quad \hat {Y} (z) = - z \frac {d}{d z} \hat {X} (z).
$$

This is because

$$
\hat {Y} (z) = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} n x (n) z ^ {- n} = \sum_ {n = - \infty} ^ {\infty} (- z) \frac {d}{d z} x (n) z ^ {- n} = - z \frac {d}{d z} \hat {X} (z).
$$

It is not difficult to show that $Roc(y)=Roc(x)$ (see Exercise 5).

This property can be used to find other Z transforms. For example, the Z transform of the unit step, $x=u$ , is $\hat{X} (z)=z / (z-1)$ , with $RoC(x)=\{z\in \mathbb{C}\mid|z|>1\}$ . So the Z transform of the unit ramp y, given by $y(n)=nu(n)$ , is

$$
\hat {Y} (z) = - z \frac {d}{d z} \frac {z}{z - 1} = \frac {z}{(z - 1) ^ {2}},
$$

with RoC(y) = {z $\in$ C $ | | z| > 1 } . Another method for finding the Z transform of the unit ramp is given in Exercise 3 of Chapter 12.

## Probing Further: Inverse transform as an integral

Even if the Z transform is not a rational polynomial, we can recover the signal x from its Z transform, $\hat{X}:RoC(x)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ , using the DTFT. A non-empty RoC(x) contains the circle of radius r for some r>0. So the series in the equation

$$
\hat {X} \left(r e ^ {i \omega}\right) = \sum_ {m = - \infty} ^ {\infty} x (m) \left(r e ^ {i \omega}\right) ^ {- m} = \sum_ {m = - \infty} ^ {\infty} \left(x (m) r ^ {- m}\right) e ^ {- i \omega m}
$$

is absolutely summable. Hence the signal $x_{r}$ : $\forall n, x_{r}(n)=x(n)r^{-n}$ , has DTFT $X_{r}:$ $\forall\omega,X_{r}(\omega)=\hat{X}(re^{i\omega})$ . We can, therefore, obtain $x_{r}$ as the inverse DTFT of $X_{r}$

$$
\forall n, \quad x _ {r} (n) = r ^ {- n} x (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \hat {X} \left(r e ^ {i \omega}\right) e ^ {i \omega n} d \omega .
$$

Multiplying both sides by $r^{n}$ , we can recover x as

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad x (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi} \hat {X} \left(r e ^ {i \omega}\right) \left(r e ^ {i \omega}\right) ^ {n} d \omega .
$$

(13.15)

This formula defines the inverse Z transform as an integral of the real variable $\omega.$ (Continued on page 601.)
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
## Probing Further: (Continued) Inverse transform

It is conventional to write the inverse Z transform differently. Express z as $z=r e^{i \omega}$ . Then as $\omega$ varies from 0 to $2\pi$ , z varies as

$$
d z = r e ^ {i \omega} i d \omega = z i d \omega , \text {o r} d \omega = \frac {d z}{i z}.
$$

Substituting this in (13.15) gives,

$$
\forall n, \quad x (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi} \oint \hat {X} (z) z ^ {n} \frac {d z}{i z} = \frac {1}{2 \pi i} \oint \hat {X} (z) z ^ {n - 1} d z.
$$

Here the 'circle' in the integral sign, $\oint$ , means that the integral in the complex z-plane is along any closed counterclockwise circle contained in $RoC(x)$ . (An integral along a closed contour is called a contour integral.) In summary,

$$
\forall n \in \mathbb {Z}, \quad x (n) = \frac {1}{2 \pi i} \oint \hat {X} (z) z ^ {n - 1} d z,
$$

(13.16)

where the integral is along any closed counterclockwise circle inside $RoC(x).$

We can similarly use the CTFT to recover any continuous-time signal x from its Laplace transform by

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad x (t) = \frac {1}{2 \pi i} \int_ {\sigma - i \infty} ^ {\sigma + i \infty} \hat {X} (s) e ^ {s t} d s
$$

where the integral is along any vertical line $(\sigma - i\infty , \sigma + i\infty)$ contained in $RoC(x)$.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
## Probing Further: Differentiation and Laplace transforms

We can use the inverse Laplace transform as given in the box on page 600 to demonstrate the differentiation property in table 13.4. Let y be defined by

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad y (t) = \frac {d}{d t} x (t).
$$

We can write x in terms of its Laplace transform as

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad x (t) = \frac {1}{2 \pi i} \int_ {\sigma - i \infty} ^ {\sigma + i \infty} \hat {X} (s) e ^ {s t} d s.
$$

Differentiating this with respect to t is easy,

$$
\forall t \in \mathbb {R}, \quad \frac {d}{d t} x (t) = \frac {1}{2 \pi i} \int_ {\sigma - i \infty} ^ {\sigma + i \infty} s \hat {X} (s) e ^ {s t} d s.
$$

Consequently, $y ( t )= d x ( t ) / d t$ is the inverse transform of $s \hat{X} ( s )$ , so

$$
\forall s \in R o C (y), \quad \hat {Y} (s) = s \hat {X} (s),
$$

RoC(y) $\supset$ RoC(x).
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

A major theme of this book is that interesting systems are often compositions of simpler systems. Systems are functions, so their composition is function composition, as discussed in section 2.1.5. However, systems are often not directly described as functions, so function composition is not the easiest tool to use to understand the composition. We have seen systems described as state machines, frequency responses, and transfer functions. In chapter 4 we obtained the state machine of the composite system from its component state machines. In section 8.5 we obtained the frequency response of the composite
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems

text:
Figure 14.1: Cascade composition of two LTI systems with transfer functions $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}.$

system from the frequency response of its component linear time-invariant (LTI) systems. We extend the latter study in this chapter to the composition of LTI systems described by their transfer functions. This important extension allows us to consider unstable systems whose impulse response has a Z or Laplace transform, but not a Fourier transform.

As before, feedback systems prove challenging. A particularly interesting issue is how to maintain stability, and how to construct stable systems out of unstable ones. We will find that some feedback compositions of stable systems result in unstable systems, and conversely, some compositions of unstable systems result in stable systems. For example, we can stabilize the helicopter in example 12.2 using feedback, in fact we can precisely control its orientation, despite the intrinsic instability. The family of techniques for doing this is known as feedback control. This chapter serves as an introduction to that topic. Feedback control can also be used to drive stable systems, in which case it serves to improve their response. For example, feedback can result in faster or more precise responses, and can also prevent overshoot, where a system overreacts to a command.

We will consider three styles of composition, cascade composition, parallel composition, and feedback composition. In each case, two LTI systems with transfer functions $\hat{H}_{1}$ and $\hat{H}_{2}$ are combined to get a new system. The transfer functions $\hat{H}_{1}$ and $\hat{H}_{2}$ are the (Z or Laplace) transforms of the respective impulse responses, $h_{1}$ and $h_{2}.$ Much of our discussion applies equally well whether the system is a continuous-time system or a discrete-time system, so in many cases we leave this unspecified.
title: Structure and Interpretation of Signals and Systems
